name: wasm-vips
baseline: jimp (pure-JavaScript image library); the same libvips compiled natively (sharp) is NOT beaten
workload: Decode, resize to 720 px wide (Lanczos3; jimp uses bicubic), re-encode in the same format: 2725x2225 JPEG, 2048x1536 PNG, 1024x772 WebP, buffer in / buffer out, Node.js, libvips cache disabled, concurrency 4.
claimed_speedup: JPEG: wasm-vips 21.30 ops/s vs jimp 3.64 ops/s (5.9x). PNG: 16.31 vs jimp 16.15 ops/s (tie, about 1.0x). WebP: 21.26 vs sharp 21.63 ops/s (tie). Versus native command-line tools on the same page: JPEG 1.2x GraphicsMagick (17.81) and 1.4x ImageMagick (15.12); PNG 1.35x gm (12.12) and 1.8x ImageMagick (9.06) (ratios derived from page data). Native sharp is faster: JPEG 84.10 ops/s, PNG 31.76 ops/s.
compiler_and_flags: Emscripten (emcc/em++, version taken from the build host and not pinned in the benchmark README). build.sh in the repo: COMMON_FLAGS -Os -pthread -fwasm-exceptions, -O3 for select dependencies, -msimd128; libjpeg-turbo built with WITH_SIMD=OFF. Benchmark: Node v25.2.1.
tradeoffs: Runs in browser and Node.js, no native binary or per-platform build. Browser use of the threaded build needs SharedArrayBuffer (cross-origin isolation). Larger download than a pure-JS library; wasm32 memory limits apply for very large images. libjpeg-turbo is built without SIMD in wasm.
caveats: Wasm-vips only beats the JavaScript equivalent (jimp) clearly on JPEG; PNG is a tie with jimp and WebP ties native sharp. The compiled-natively counterpart (sharp, libvips) is 3.9x faster on JPEG and 1.9x faster on PNG, so this is a win over JS and over some native CLI tools, not over native libvips. jimp row is not like for like (bicubic instead of Lanczos3; no premultiply on PNG; no WebP support). Node.js only, no in-browser run in the table. Author's own benchmark (derived from sharp's suite); compiler version not stated on the benchmark page. A 2020 libvips.org post reported different ratios (sharp 8.3x JPEG, wasm-vips 5.9x vs jimp JPEG); that post could not be opened here.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'wasm-vips OR libvips WebAssembly benchmark faster than sharp OR canvas OR JavaScript image processing in the browser' surfaced the libvips.org post 'libvips for WebAssembly' (host unreachable here, snippet only); numbers taken from the repo's test/bench README opened on raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: libxml2-wasm
baseline: libxmljs2 (native Node binding of libxml2) and pure-JavaScript XML parsers (@rgrove/parse-xml, fast-xml-parser, xmldoc)
workload: DOM tree parsing of three XML documents (780 bytes, 35,562 bytes, 2,337,522 bytes) in Node.js, ops/s via the repo's benchmark/ suite.
claimed_speedup: Buffer API vs libxmljs2: 167,479 vs 78,688 ops/s on the small file (2.1x), 17,114 vs 12,414 on the medium file (1.4x), 62 vs 50 on the large file (1.2x). Buffer API vs @rgrove/parse-xml: 2.1x, 3.4x and 3.3x; vs fast-xml-parser: 3.2x, 6.3x, 3.9x (ratios derived from page data). The String API is slower than libxmljs2 on medium (6,013 vs 12,414 ops/s) and large (43 vs 50) files.
compiler_and_flags: Emscripten (version not stated). package.json: libxml2 configured --without-sax1 --without-modules --without-html --without-threads --without-catalog --without-debug with CFLAGS=-O2; link flags in binding/emcc.txt: -O2 -flto --closure 1 -s ALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH=1 -s SINGLE_FILE=1. Benchmark run on Node.js v18.19.0.
tradeoffs: Speed advantage requires the Buffer API (UTF-8 input); the String API pays a UTF-16 to UTF-8 conversion. Documents must be freed with dispose() or memory leaks. Built without HTML, SAX1, modules, catalogs and threads, so those libxml2 features are not available. Needs ES modules and top-level await. Runs in browsers, unlike the native binding.
caveats: Single machine and a Node 18 era run; the benchmark date is not stated. libxmljs2 build (prebuilt or local) and compiler flags are not stated, and Emscripten version is not pinned. Margin over native libxmljs2 shrinks to 1.2x on the 2.3 MB file, and the String API loses to native on larger inputs. First-party benchmark by the library author; the report prints ops/s with a relative error margin but does not state warm-up or iteration policy.
found_via: Blogs / talks: registry text search (npm search API 'emscripten compiled c library faster', 'wasm port faster than pure js') surfaced libxml2-wasm; README footnote led to docs/performance.md.

name: @mtcute/wasm (mtcute)
baseline: pako (pure JS zlib) and Node.js built-in zlib for deflate/gunzip; @cryptography/aes (pure JS) for AES-IGE/CTR
workload: Randomised JSON payloads of about 48 B, 443 B, 13 KB, 73 KB and 545 KB (MTProto usage sizes): deflate, gunzip, AES-IGE, AES-CTR, SHA-1, SHA-256 in Node.js, each test in its own child process, 2 s warm-up then 10 runs of 1 s.
claimed_speedup: README of @mtcute/wasm: 'up to 10x faster than pure JS implementations'. results.md, 73 KB payload: gunzip libdeflate-wasm 345.6 MB/s vs pako 63.5 MB/s (5.4x, derived) and Node zlib 228.9 MB/s (1.5x, derived); deflate 34.6 vs pako 10.9 (3.2x) and zlib 16.9 (2.0x); AES-IGE tgcrypto-wasm about 135 MB/s encrypt vs @cryptography/aes 57.8 (2.3x); AES-CTR 137.1 vs 87.5 MB/s (1.6x); SHA-1 teeny-sha1-wasm 280.6 vs rusha 137.7 MB/s (2.0x).
compiler_and_flags: Shipped package (packages/wasm/lib/Makefile): clang 16 on Alpine 3.18.4, -target wasm32-unknown-unknown -O3 -flto=full -fno-inline -fno-unroll-loops -mbulk-memory, wasm-opt available; the benchmark repo builds its own libdeflate/tgcrypto blobs (plain and no-unroll variants) and does not state the flags. Node.js v18.17.1.
stars_or_usage: 570 stars (mtcute repo); TypeScript MTProto library used by Telegram bots and web clients
tradeoffs: 47 KB raw / 24 KB gzipped wasm. AES-IGE code derives from tgcrypto (LGPL-3.0, source kept in the lib/crypto directory), deflate is a modified libdeflate (MIT), so the licensing is mixed. Optional SIMD blob.
caveats: Wins are against pure JS and, for libdeflate, against Node's zlib only at medium and larger payloads; at the tiny payload fast-zlib (8.0 MB/s) beats libdeflate-wasm (3.9 MB/s) on deflate. Native OpenSSL is far faster than the wasm crypto (AES-CTR 1,791 MB/s vs 137 MB/s on 73 KB; SHA-256 1,065 vs 223) and tgcrypto as a Node addon beats the wasm build (236 vs 135 MB/s IGE); the author's own conclusion is to use native crypto on Node and wasm elsewhere. Benchmarks are by the library author; the benchmark repo was last updated 2023-11-07 on Node 18; libdeflate compression level is not stated and output sizes differ slightly (64.65% vs 64.94% for zlib on 73 KB).
found_via: Blogs / talks: npm registry scan of wasm packages for 'faster than pure JS' claims found @mtcute/wasm ('Up to 10x faster than pure JS implementations'); README pointed to github.com/mtcute/benchmarks.

name: brepkit
baseline: OpenCASCADE (OCCT) compiled to WebAssembly (occt-wasm 3.8.3), both through the brepjs adapter
workload: Nine B-rep CAD operations on small test solids in single-threaded Node.js: fuse of two boxes, box minus cylinder, box chamfer, box fillet, box-sphere intersect, 16-hole multi-boolean, sphere tessellation, box volume, STEP export; median of 5 iterations after 2 warm-ups, every row output-verified before timing.
claimed_speedup: brepkit (wasm) vs OCCT (wasm): fuse(box,box) x10 0.43 ms vs 44.9 ms (103x); cut(box,cylinder) x10 19.2 vs 64.9 ms (3.4x); box+chamfer 0.10 vs 5.6 ms (55x); box+fillet 0.33 vs 6.1 ms (18x); intersect(box,sphere) x10 0.23 vs 59.1 ms (252x); multi-boolean 4.6 vs 30.3 ms (6.6x); mesh sphere 6.2 vs 49.4 ms (7.9x); volume x100 0.18 vs 9.8 ms (54x); exportSTEP x10 0.85 vs 14.3 ms (17x).
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.88+, cargo build -p brepkit-wasm --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release (wasm-opt settings not stated); occt-wasm build flags not stated. Released npm packages exact-pinned in the brepkit-bench lockfile: brepkit-wasm 3.0.0, occt-wasm 3.8.3, brepjs 18.120.0.
hardware: Linux x86_64, CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 32 stars; npm package brepkit-wasm, crate brepkit-operations
tradeoffs: Different kernel, not a port of OCCT: feature coverage is narrower (IGES is experimental, PLY import not exposed in wasm). AGPL-3.0-only with a commercial licence for proprietary embedding and a contributor licence agreement; versions through 2.129.x were MIT OR Apache-2.0. Native Rust build is faster still than the wasm build.
caveats: First-party numbers; CPU model not stated; the OCCT wasm baseline (occt-wasm) is built by the same author, whose build settings are not stated. Small primitive test shapes; boolean and STEP rows are batches of ten operations. No native OCCT baseline is reported. The comparison goes through a shared adapter layer that may add per-call overhead for both sides.
found_via: Blogs / talks: npm registry scan of wasm packages (occt-wasm search result) led to the brepkit README Performance section; harness repo andymai/brepkit-bench is linked there.

name: contour-wasm
baseline: MarchingSquares.js isoBands (pure JavaScript, used internally by turf-isobands)
workload: Isoband computation on grids of 5,307 to 1,010,880 points with 14 to 23 intervals.
claimed_speedup: 5,307 points / 23 intervals: 16 ms vs 12 ms; 17,608 / 15: 25 vs 15 ms; 336,960 / 14: 369 vs 186 ms; 1,010,880 / 14: 832 vs 492 ms (about 1.3x to 2.0x faster, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0-or-later (from Cargo.toml) restricts embedding in closed web apps. Rust compiled with wasm-pack; needs async wasm initialisation. Isobands and isolines only.
caveats: Micro-benchmark in the README with no hardware, browser or Node version, no flags and no link to the benchmark code; four data points; speedup shrinks to 1.3x on small inputs, where wasm call overhead matters. Repo has had no commits since 2024-03-11. Results may predate recent MarchingSquares.js versions.
found_via: Blogs / talks: npm registry scan of wasm-related packages (README grep for benchmark tables mentioning JavaScript baselines).

name: blake3.wasm (UneBaguette)
workload: BLAKE3 hashing of 32 B, 1 KB, 64 KB, 1 MB and 10 MB inputs in Node.js v24, compared with @noble/hashes, awasm-noble and awasm-noble with threads.
claimed_speedup: Apple M4: blake3-wasm vs @noble/hashes 129 vs 28 MB/s at 32 B (4.6x), 568 vs 105 at 1 KB (5.4x), 2,004 vs 102 at 64 KB (19.6x), 1,893 vs 101 at 1 MB (18.7x), 2,185 vs 101 at 10 MB (21.6x). Ryzen 7 5800X: 2,067 vs 52 MB/s at 64 KB (39.7x) and 1,776 vs 50 at 10 MB (35.5x) (ratios derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README (make build; Rust to wasm); Node.js v24
tradeoffs: Wasm module needs async initialisation and manual or finaliser-based freeing of hasher objects (README warns about double free with using). The README itself notes the JavaScript boundary adds non-determinism and points to blake3-napi, a native addon that is faster for large inputs.
caveats: First-party table with no benchmark command or script path in the README and no compiler flags. The @noble/hashes baseline is a deliberately small pure-JS library; native blake3 (Rust crate or the blake3 npm package) is not in the table. Two hardware sets but a single run each.
found_via: Blogs / talks: npm registry scan of wasm packages; README benchmark table compared against @noble/hashes and awasm-noble.

name: awasm-noble
workload: BLAKE3 hashing of 32 B to 10 MB inputs in Node.js v24; awasm-noble wasm and wasm_threads backends vs @noble/hashes, measured in the README of the third-party blake3.wasm repo.
claimed_speedup: Third-party table (Apple M4): awasm-noble 843 vs @noble/hashes 105 MB/s at 1 KB (8.0x), 1,898 vs 102 at 64 KB (18.6x), 1,943 vs 101 at 1 MB (19.2x), threaded 4,711 vs 101 at 1 MB (46.6x). Ryzen 7 5800X: 1,729 vs 52 MB/s at 64 KB (33x), threaded 4,946 vs 50 at 10 MB (about 99x) (ratios derived from page data). The awasm-noble README itself states '6-10 GB/s for BLAKE3' on an Apple M4 and gives no baseline.
compiler_and_flags: Auditable JS-to-wasm compiler in the repo (wasm SIMD, optional web-worker threads); no flags; Node.js v24
hardware: Apple M4; AMD Ryzen 7 5800X (third-party table). Own README: Apple M4
stars_or_usage: 52 stars; by the author of noble-hashes
tradeoffs: Wasm backends need the wasm-unsafe-eval content-security-policy; the threaded backend needs cross-origin isolation headers (COOP and COEP). Offers wasm, wasm_threads, js, noble, webcrypto and runtime backends behind one API, so apps can fall back. Wasm binaries are reproducibly generated from JS source for auditing.
caveats: The baseline comparison is not in awasm-noble's own README; it comes from another author's repo and covers only BLAKE3, so the numbers for other algorithms against @noble/hashes are unconfirmed. Wasm figures at 32 B are close to the JS baseline overhead. No native baseline. Confidence reflects the second-hand source.
found_via: Blogs / talks: found as a comparison column in the README benchmark table of UneBaguette/blake3.wasm during a wasm npm-package scan; then opened awasm-noble README and Speed section.

name: fast-theta
baseline: cos-similarity, fast-cosine-similarity and compute-cosine-similarity (JavaScript npm packages)
workload: Cosine similarity (dot product of pre-normalized vectors) for 384, 768 and 1536-dimension vectors, Node.js and browser benchmark scripts in the repo.
claimed_speedup: 384 dims: 3.3M ops/s vs cos-similarity 1.8M (1.8x), fast-cosine-similarity 1.4M (2.4x), compute-cosine-similarity 503K (6.6x). 768 dims: 2.6M vs 1.1M, 847K, 260K. 1536 dims: 1.8M vs 597K (3.0x), 414K, 134K (13x) (ratios derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Hand-written WAT compiled with the repo's compile-wat step; f32x4 SIMD, 4x unrolled with independent accumulators
tradeoffs: Needs WebAssembly SIMD. Vectors must be normalized first (normalize() call) for the headline number. Wasm binary under 1 KB embedded as base64.
caveats: The headline row measures a bare dot product on pre-normalized vectors, while the JS libraries compute a full cosine similarity including the normalization, so the comparison is not like for like. No CPU, browser or Node version stated; no versions of the JS baselines. License is declared MIT in package.json and on npm but the repo has no LICENSE file.
found_via: Blogs / talks: npm registry scan of wasm packages (README grep for 'ops/s' tables comparing against JS libraries).
